arXiv:1910.03494v1 [math.AG] 08 Oct 2019
Abstract.

This paper considers the family 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} of smooth affine factorial surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 0 with trivial units over an algebraically closed field kk. Our main result (Theorem 4.1) is that the number of isomorphism classes represented in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is at least countably infinite. This contradicts the earlier classification of Gurjar and Miyanishi [5] which asserted that 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} has at most two elements up to isomorphism when k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. Thus, the classification of surfaces in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} for the field ℂ\mathbb{C}, long thought to have been settled, is an open problem.

Key words and phrases: 
factorial surface, affine surface, logarithmic Kodaira dimension
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R05, 14J26

1. Introduction

Let kk be an algebraically closed field kk, and let 𝒮\mathscr{S} denote the family of smooth affine factorial surfaces with trivial units over kk. Then 𝒮\mathscr{S} is partitioned according to logarithmic Kodaira dimension:

𝒮=𝒮2∪𝒮1∪𝒮0∪𝒮−∞\mathscr{S}=\mathscr{S}_{2}\cup\mathscr{S}_{1}\cup\mathscr{S}_{0}\cup\mathscr{S}_{-\infty}

where S∈𝒮dS\in\mathscr{S}_{d} means κ¯​(S)=d\bar{\kappa}(S)=d. Surfaces in 𝒮2\mathscr{S}_{2} are said to be of general type. It is known that 𝒮−∞\mathscr{S}_{-\infty} consists of one element (up to isomorphism), namely, the affine plane 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}; see [7].

In their 1988 paper [5], Gurjar and Miyanishi studied elements of 𝒮\mathscr{S} of non-general type in the case k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. For 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0}, they claim that “there are only two types of surfaces in this case” (p.99). Specifically, Theorem 2 asserts that any element of 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is isomorphic to one of the surfaces SS or S′S^{\prime}, defined as follows. Let x,yx,y be a system of coordinate functions in the complex plane ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.

  • •

    SS is obtained by blowing up ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} at the points (0,1)(0,1) and (1,0)(1,0), and removing the proper transform of the degenerate conic defined by x​y=0xy=0.

  • •

    S′S^{\prime} is obtained by blowing up ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} the point (1,1)(1,1), and removing the proper transform of the smooth conic x​y=1xy=1.

In this paper, we will show the following.

  1. (1)

    S≅ℂS′S\cong_{\mathbb{C}}S^{\prime}   (Theorem 4.4)

  2. (2)

    For any algebraically closed field kk, the number of isomorphism classes represented in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is at least countably infinite.

In fact, even the number of stable isomorphism classes represented in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is at least countably infinite (see Theorem 5.1). Thus, the classification of surfaces in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} for the field ℂ\mathbb{C}, long thought to have been settled, is an open problem.

The surface S′S^{\prime} is the affine modification of the plane along the curve x​y=1xy=1 with center (1,1)(1,1); see [6]. For any algebraically closed field kk, the curve x​y=1xy=1 is isomorphic to the affine line over kk with one point removed, denoted 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}. But this is just one of many ways to embed 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*} in 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}, and each of these embeddings, together with a point on the curve, yields an affine modification XX of 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}. Theorem 3.1 gives conditions on the embedding which imply that X∈𝒮X\in\mathscr{S}, and Theorem 3.2 gives further conditions which imply X∈𝒮0X\in\mathscr{S}_{0}.

We consider the family of embeddings xn​y=1x^{n}y=1, n≥1n\geq 1. Specifically, let VnV_{n} be the affine modification of 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} along the curve Γn\Gamma_{n} defined by xn​y=1x^{n}y=1 with center (1,1)(1,1). We show that Vn∈𝒮0V_{n}\in\mathscr{S}_{0} for each n≥1n\geq 1, and that Vm≇VnV_{m}\not\cong V_{n} if m≠nm\neq n, and more generally, for cylinders over these surfaces, Vm×𝔸kd≇Vn×𝔸kdV_{m}\times\mathbb{A}^{d}_{k}\not\cong V_{n}\times\mathbb{A}^{d}_{k} if m≠nm\neq n and d≥0d\geq 0; see Theorem 5.1.

For each nn, we have Γn≅𝔸∗1\Gamma_{n}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, but it is not hard to show that the complements 𝔸k2∖Γm\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}\setminus\Gamma_{m} and 𝔸k2∖Γn\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}\setminus\Gamma_{n} are not isomorphic when m≠nm\neq n. Consequently, there is no automorphism of 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} transforming Γm\Gamma_{m} to Γn\Gamma_{n} when m≠nm\neq n. For the field k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, the closed embeddings of ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{*} in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} have been classified (see [2]), thus providing a rich family of surfaces to study, obtained by affine modification of ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2}.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Some Notation

If RR is an integral domain, then frac⁡(R){\rm frac}(R) is the field of fractions of RR. Given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, R[n]R^{[n]} is the polynomial ring in nn variables over RR, and R[±n]R^{[\pm n]} is the ring of Laurent polynomials in nn variables over RR. If SS is an integral domain containing RR, then tr.degR​S{\rm tr.deg}_{R}S is the transcendence degree of frac⁡(S){\rm frac}(S) over frac⁡(R){\rm frac}(R).

Assume that kk is algebraically closed. Given distinct c1,…,cn∈kc_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\in k, let

𝔸∗n1​(k)=𝔸∗n1=Spec​k​[t,(t−c1)−1,…,(t−cn)−1]\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*n}(k)=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*n}={\rm Spec}\,k[t,(t-c_{1})^{-1},\ldots,(t-c_{n})^{-1}]

i.e., an affine line over kk with nn points removed. If n=1n=1, we also write 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}. Given d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, 𝔸kd\mathbb{A}^{d}_{k} denotes affine space over kk of dimension dd.

2.2. The Degree-Neutral Invariant

Let RR be an integral domain, and let deg:R→ℤ∪{−∞}\deg:R\to\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty\} be a degree function. We say deg\deg is non-negative if deg\deg is of the form deg:R→ℕ∪{−∞}\deg:R\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{-\infty\}, and trivial if deg⁡(R∖{0})={0}\deg(R\setminus\{0\})=\{0\}. The induced filtration is

R=⋃d∈ℤℱdR=\bigcup_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{F}_{d}

where the sets ℱd={r∈R|deg⁡r≤d}\mathcal{F}_{d}=\{r\in R\,|\,\deg r\leq d\} are the associated degree modules. Note that deg\deg can be extended to K=frac⁡(R)K={\rm frac}(R) by letting deg⁡(f/g)=deg⁡f−deg⁡g\deg(f/g)=\deg f-\deg g for f,g∈Rf,g\in R, g≠0g\neq 0. Note also that, if RR is a field, then deg\deg is a degree function on RR if and only if (−deg)(-\deg) is a discrete valuation of RR.

Recall that a subalgebra A⊂RA\subset R is factorially closed in RR if r​s∈Ars\in A for nonzero r,s∈Rr,s\in R implies r∈Ar\in A and s∈As\in A.

Proposition 2.1.

With the assumptions and notation above:

  • (a)

    ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is a subring of RR which is integrally closed in RR.

  • (b)

    ℱd\mathcal{F}_{d} is an ideal of ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} for each d≤0d\leq 0.

  • (c)

    If deg\deg is non-negative, then ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is factorially closed in RR. Consequently, R∗⊂ℱ0R^{*}\subset\mathcal{F}_{0}.

  • (d)

    If RR is a normal ring, then ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is a normal ring.

  • (e)

    If RR is a field, then ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is a valuation ring of RR and frac⁡(ℱ0)=R{\rm frac}(\mathcal{F}_{0})=R.

Proof.

Extend deg\deg to KK and let V={f∈K|deg⁡f≤0}V=\{f\in K\,|\,\deg f\leq 0\}. Then VV is a valuation ring of KK, and ℱ0=V∩R\mathcal{F}_{0}=V\cap R. This implies parts (a), (d) and (e), and part (b) is clear. For part (c), if a​b∈ℱ0ab\in\mathcal{F}_{0} for nonzero a,b∈Ra,b\in R, then 0=deg⁡(a​b)=deg⁡a+deg⁡b0=\deg(ab)=\deg a+\deg b in ℕ\mathbb{N} implies deg⁡a=deg⁡b=0\deg a=\deg b=0, so a,b∈ℱ0a,b\in\mathcal{F}_{0}. ∎

Definition 2.2.

The degree-neutral invariant of RR is the subring of RR defined by the intersection of all subrings of the form ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} for some non-negative degree function on RR, denoted by Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(R). We say that RR is degree-rigid if Δ0​(R)=R\Delta^{0}(R)=R, i.e., every non-negative degree function on RR is trivial.

The degree-neutral invariant has the following properties.

  1. (1)

    Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(R) is a factorially closed subring of RR, being the intersection of factorially closed subrings, and Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(R) is an invariant subring of RR. Therefore, Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(R) is an algebraically closed subring of RR, and if RR is a UFD, then Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(R) is a UFD.

  2. (2)

    R∗⊂Δ0​(R)R^{*}\subset\Delta^{0}(R).

  3. (3)

    If S⊂RS\subset R is a subring, then Δ0​(S)⊂Δ0​(R)\Delta^{0}(S)\subset\Delta^{0}(R), since any non-negative degree function on RR restricts to a non-negative degree function on SS.

  4. (4)

    If R⁡[x1,…,xn]≅R[n]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\cong R^{[n]}, then by considering the degree functions degzi\deg_{z_{i}}, 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, it is clear that Δ0​(R[n])⊂R\Delta^{0}\left(R^{[n]}\right)\subset R.

  5. (5)

    The Makar-Limanov invariant M​L​(R)ML(R) is defined by the intersection of subrings of the form ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} for certain non-negative degree functions; see [3, 4]. Therefore, Δ0​(R)⊂M​L​(R)\Delta^{0}(R)\subset ML(R). RR is said to be rigid if M​L​(R)=RML(R)=R. Thus, degree-rigid implies rigid.

Recall that RR is strongly invariant if the following condition holds (see [1]).

For any integer n≥0n\geq 0 and subring S⊂R⁡[x1,…,xn]≅R[n]S\subset R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\cong R^{[n]}, if there exist y1,…,yny_{1},\ldots,y_{n} in R[n]R^{[n]} such that R⁡[x1,…,xn]=S⁡[y1,…,yn]R[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=S[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}], then R=SR=S.

Lemma 2.3.

Suppose that RR is degree-rigid.

  • (a)

    Δ0​(R[n])=R\Delta^{0}(R^{[n]})=R

  • (b)

    RR is strongly invariant.

Proof.

Let δ\delta be a non-negative degree function on R[n]R^{[n]} with induced filtration ⋃i∈ℕℱi\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i}. Then δ\delta restricts to RR, so δ⁡(f)=0\delta(f)=0 every f∈R∖{0}f\in R\setminus\{0\}, and R⊂ℱ0R\subset\mathcal{F}_{0}. Therefore, R⊂Δ0​(R[n])⊂RR\subset\Delta^{0}(R^{[n]})\subset R, which implies Δ0​(R[n])=R\Delta^{0}(R^{[n]})=R. This shows part (a).

For part (b), assume that BB is a ring containing RR, and B≅RR[n]B\cong_{R}R^{[n]} for some n≥0n\geq 0. Let S⊂BS\subset B be a subring such that B≅SS[n]B\cong_{S}S^{[n]}. Then R=Δ0​(B)⊂S⊂R[n]R=\Delta^{0}(B)\subset S\subset R^{[n]}. Therefore, tr.degR​S≤n{\rm tr.deg}_{R}S\leq n and:

n=tr.degR​B=tr.degR​S+tr.degS​B=tr.degR​S+n⟹tr.degR​S=0n={\rm tr.deg}_{R}B={\rm tr.deg}_{R}S+{\rm tr.deg}_{S}B={\rm tr.deg}_{R}S+n\implies{\rm tr.deg}_{R}S=0

Since both SS and RR are algebraically closed in BB, it follows that RR is algebraically closed in SS. Therefore, R=SR=S. ∎

2.3. Samuel’s Criterion

A well known criterion for a ring to be a UFD is given by Samuel [8], Proposition 7.6. In an integral domain AA, elements a,b∈Aa,b\in A are relatively prime if a​A∩b​A=a​b​AaA\cap bA=abA.

Proposition 2.4.

Assume that AA is an integral domain and a,b∈Aa,b\in A are relatively prime and nonzero. Let A⁡[X]≅A[1]A[X]\cong A^{[1]} and A′=A⁡[X]/(a​X−b)A^{\prime}=A[X]/(aX-b).

  • (a)

    a​X−baX-b is a prime element of A⁡[X]A[X].

  • (b)

    If AA is a noetherian UFD and a​AaA and a​A+b​AaA+bA are prime ideals of AA, then A′A^{\prime} is a noetherian UFD.

3. Surfaces defined by 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*} Embeddings

In this section, we use certain closed embeddings of the punctured line 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*} in the plane 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} to define surfaces belonging to 𝒮\mathscr{S}.

3.1. A Family of Surfaces in 𝒮\mathscr{S}

Theorem 3.1.

Let A=k⁡[x,y]≅k[2]A=k[x,y]\cong k^{[2]} and let a,b∈Aa,b\in A be such that:

A/a​A≅k[±1],A/b​A≅k[1],A/(a​A+b​A)≅kA/aA\cong k^{[\pm 1]}\,\,,\,\,A/bA\cong k^{[1]}\,\,,\,\,A/(aA+bA)\cong k

Define the ring B⊂AaB\subset A_{a} by B=A⁡[b/a]B=A[b/a].

  • (a)

    BB is a UFD and B∗=k∗B^{*}=k^{*}.

  • (b)

    If kk is algebraically closed and X=Spec⁡(B)X={\rm Spec}(B), then X∈𝒮X\in\mathscr{S}.

Proof.

We have B≅A⁡[X]/(a​X−b)B\cong A[X]/(aX-b), where A⁡[X]≅A[1]A[X]\cong A^{[1]}. In addition, aa and bb are prime elements of AA, gcdA⁡(a,b)=1\gcd_{A}(a,b)=1 and the ideal a​A+b​AaA+bA is prime in AA. By Samuel’s Criterion, it follows that BB is a UFD. Since A⊂B⊂AaA\subset B\subset A_{a} and B≠AaB\neq A_{a}, we see that B∗=A∗=k∗B^{*}=A^{*}=k^{*}. This proves part (a).

To prove part (b), let Γ⊂𝔸2\Gamma\subset\mathbb{A}^{2} be the curve defined by a=0a=0, noting that Γ≅𝔸∗1\Gamma\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}. Define the maximal ideal I=(a,b)⊂AI=(a,b)\subset A, and let P∈𝔸k2P\in\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} be the point defined by II, noting that P∈ΓP\in\Gamma. Let WW be the blow-up of 𝔸k2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} at PP. Then WW is smooth. Let Γ′⊂W\Gamma^{\prime}\subset W be the proper transform of Γ\Gamma. Then W∖Γ′W\setminus\Gamma^{\prime} is smooth, and the coordinate ring of W∖Γ′W\setminus\Gamma^{\prime} is the affine modification:

A⁡[a−1​I]=A⁡[a−1​(a,b)]=A⁡[b/a]=BA[a^{-1}I]=A[a^{-1}(a,b)]=A[b/a]=B

Therefore, X=W∖Γ′X=W\setminus\Gamma^{\prime} is smooth, which implies X∈𝒮X\in\mathscr{S}. ∎

3.2. Logarithmic Kodaira Dimension

Assume that the ground field kk is algebraically closed. Let B=A⁡[b/a]B=A[b/a] be a ring of the type described in Theorem 3.1, that is, A=k⁡[x,y]≅k[2]A=k[x,y]\cong k^{[2]} and a,b∈Aa,b\in A are such that:

A/a​A≅k[±1],A/b​A≅k[1],A/(a​A+b​A)≅kA/aA\cong k^{[\pm 1]}\,\,,\,\,A/bA\cong k^{[1]}\,\,,\,\,A/(aA+bA)\cong k

Let X=Spec⁡(B)X={\rm Spec}(B). By Theorem 3.1, X∈𝒮X\in\mathscr{S}.

Theorem 3.2.

Let Γ⊂𝔸k2\Gamma\subset\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} be the curve defined by the ideal a​AaA.

  • (a)

    κ¯​(X)=κ¯​(𝔸k2∖Γ)\bar{\kappa}(X)=\bar{\kappa}(\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}\setminus\Gamma)

  • (b)

    If Γ\Gamma has two places at infinity, then κ¯​(X)≥0\bar{\kappa}(X)\geq 0.

  • (c)

    If the complement 𝔸k2∖Γ\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}\setminus\Gamma contains an open set isomorphic to 𝔸∗1×𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, then κ¯​(X)≤0\bar{\kappa}(X)\leq 0.

In order to prove the theorem, we need the following lemma, which is well-known.

Lemma 3.3.

Let VV be a smooth projective surface defined over kk and let CC be a reduced curve on VV. Let π:W→V\pi:W\to V be the blow-up at a point PP on CC and let DD be the proper transform of CC on WW. If PP is a smooth point of CC, then κ¯​(W∖D)=κ¯​(V∖C)\bar{\kappa}(W\setminus D)=\bar{\kappa}(V\setminus C).

Proof.

We may assume that CC is an SNC-divisor, i.e., CC has only normal crossings and consists of smooth curves. Since PP is a smooth point of CC, we have KW+D∼π∗​(KV+C)K_{W}+D\sim\pi^{*}(K_{V}+C). So H0​(W,𝒪W​(n⁡(KW+D)))≅H0​(V,𝒪V​(n⁡(KV+C)))H^{0}(W,\mathcal{O}_{W}(n(K_{W}+D)))\cong H^{0}(V,\mathcal{O}_{V}(n(K_{V}+C))) for any integer n≥1n\geq 1. Hence, κ¯​(W∖D)=κ¯​(V∖C)\bar{\kappa}(W\setminus D)=\bar{\kappa}(V\setminus C). ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Let S=𝔸k2∖ΓS=\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k}\setminus\Gamma, let P∈𝔸k2P\in\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} be the point defined by the maximal ideal (a,b)(a,b), let π:W→𝔸k2\pi:W\to\mathbb{A}^{2}_{k} be the blow-up at the point PP, and let Γ′⊂W\Gamma^{\prime}\subset W be the proper transform of Γ\Gamma. Then X≅W∖Γ′X\cong W\setminus\Gamma^{\prime}. Since PP is a smooth point of Γ\Gamma, we infer from Lemma 3.3 that

κ¯​(X)=κ¯​(W∖Γ′)=κ¯​(S)\bar{\kappa}(X)=\bar{\kappa}(W\setminus\Gamma^{\prime})=\bar{\kappa}(S)

This proves part (a).

For part (b), since Γ\Gamma is a smooth affine plane curve with two places at infinity, the log geometric genus of SS is positive; see, e.g., Chapter 2, Lemma 2.2.2 (p. 72) of [7]. Hence, κ¯​(S)≥0\bar{\kappa}(S)\geq 0, so κ¯​(X)≥0\bar{\kappa}(X)\geq 0.

For part (c), since SS contains an open set U≅𝔸∗1×𝔸∗1U\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, we have κ¯​(S)≤κ¯​(𝔸∗1×𝔸∗1)=0\bar{\kappa}(S)\leq\bar{\kappa}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*})=0. Therefore, κ¯​(X)≤0\bar{\kappa}(X)\leq 0. ∎

4. The Rings BnB_{n}

4.1. Definition

Let A=k⁡[x,y]≅k[2]A=k[x,y]\cong k^{[2]}. Given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, n≥0n\geq 0, define the ring:

Bn=A⁡[(x−1)/(xn​y−1)]B_{n}=A[(x-1)/(x^{n}y-1)]

By Theorem 3.1, we see that BnB_{n} is a UFD and Bn∗=k∗B_{n}^{*}=k^{*}. Let u=(x−1)/(xn​y−1)u=(x-1)/(x^{n}y-1).

4.2. Fibrations

Assume that kk is algebraically closed, and fix the positive integer nn. Let Vn=Spec⁡(Bn)V_{n}={\rm Spec}(B_{n}). Given λ∈k\lambda\in k, consider the fibers x−λx-\lambda, u−λu-\lambda and y−λy-\lambda. There are three cases.

  1. (1)

    General fiber: λ∉{0,1}\lambda\not\in\{0,1\}

    (i) Spec​B/(x−λ)≅Spec​k​[y,u]/(u⁡(λn​y−1)+(1−λ))≅𝔸∗1{\rm Spec}\,B/(x-\lambda)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[y,u]/(u(\lambda^{n}y-1)+(1-\lambda))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}

    (ii) Spec​B/(u−λ)≅Spec​k​[x,y]/(λ⁡(xn​y−1)−(x−1))≅𝔸∗1{\rm Spec}\,B/(u-\lambda)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[x,y]/(\lambda(x^{n}y-1)-(x-1))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}

    (iii) Spec​B/(y−λ)≅Spec​k​[x,u]/(u⁡(λ​xn−1)−(x−1))≅𝔸∗n1{\rm Spec}\,B/(y-\lambda)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[x,u]/(u(\lambda x^{n}-1)-(x-1))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*n}

  2. (2)

    Reducible fiber: λ=1\lambda=1

    (i) Spec​B/(x−1)≅Spec​k​[y,u]/(u⁡(y−1))≅𝔸k1∪𝔸k1{\rm Spec}\,B/(x-1)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[y,u]/(u(y-1))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}

    (ii) Spec​B/(u−1)≅Spec​k​[x,y]/(x⁡(xn−1​y−1))≅𝔸k1∪𝔸∗1{\rm Spec}\,B/(u-1)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[x,y]/(x(x^{n-1}y-1))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}

    (iii) Spec​B/(y−1)≅Spec​k​[x,u]/((x−1)​(u⁡(xn−1+⋯+x+1)−1))≅𝔸k1∪𝔸∗(n−1)1{\rm Spec}\,B/(y-1)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[x,u]/((x-1)(u(x^{n-1}+\cdots+x+1)-1))\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*(n-1)}

  3. (3)

    Zero fiber: λ=0\lambda=0

    (i) Spec​B/(x)≅Spec​k​[y]≅𝔸k1{\rm Spec}\,B/(x)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[y]\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}

    (ii) Spec​B/(u)≅Spec​k​[y]≅𝔸k1{\rm Spec}\,B/(u)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[y]\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}

    (iii) Spec​B/(y)≅Spec​k​[x]≅𝔸k1{\rm Spec}\,B/(y)\cong{\rm Spec}\,k[x]\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}

Note that the inclusions k⁡[x]→Bnk[x]\to B_{n} and k⁡[u]→Bnk[u]\to B_{n} induce 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}-fibrations of VnV_{n}. Note also that the ideals (x−λ)(x-\lambda), (u−λ)(u-\lambda) and (y−λ)(y-\lambda) are prime if and only if λ≠1\lambda\neq 1.

Given m,n∈ℕ∖{0}m,n\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{0\}, if Bm≅kBnB_{m}\cong_{k}B_{n}, then m=nm=n.

The degree function restricts to BB. Let B=⋃d∈ℤℱdB=\bigcup_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{F}_{d} be the filtration of BB by degree modules. We claim that the following two properties hold:

(2) h∈B​and​deg⁡h<0⟹h∈y​Bh\in B\,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\deg h<0\implies h\in yB

and

(3) h∈B​is​prime​and​deg⁡h<0⟹h​B=y​B​and​k​[h]=k⁡[y]h\in B\,\,\,{\rm is\,\,prime\,\,and}\,\,\deg h<0\implies hB=yB\,\,{\rm and}\,\,k[h]=k[y]

To prove these implications, note that, since BB is a UFD, yy is prime in BB and y​B+t​B=ByB+tB=B, it follows that y​Bt∩B=y​ByB_{t}\cap B=yB. Therefore, if h∈Bh\in B and deg⁡h<0\deg h<0, then h∈y​Bth\in yB_{t} by the implication (1). But then h∈y​Bt∩B=y​Bh\in yB_{t}\cap B=yB. So the implication (2) is confirmed.

Suppose h∈Bh\in B is prime and deg⁡h<0\deg h<0. Then by (2) we have h​B=y​BhB=yB, since yy is prime in BB. Since B∗=k∗B^{*}=k^{*}, it follows that k⁡[h]=k⁡[y]k[h]=k[y]. So the implication (3) is confirmed.

Since YY is prime and the general fiber of YY is 𝔸∗n1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*n}, and since 𝔸∗n1≇𝔸∗m1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*n}\not\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*m}, it follows that deg⁡Y≥0\deg Y\geq 0.

In addition, UU is prime, the general fiber of UU is 𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, and the reducible fiber of UU is 𝔸k1∪𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}. If deg⁡U<0\deg U<0, then 𝔸∗1=𝔸∗m1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*m} implies m=1m=1. But then the reducible fibers give 𝔸k1∪𝔸k1≅𝔸1∪𝔸∗1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{k}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\cup\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}, a contradiction. So deg⁡U≥0\deg U\geq 0.

Since Xn​Y−1X^{n}Y-1 is prime and has a reducible fiber with n+1>2n+1>2 components, it follows that deg⁡(Xn​Y−1)≥0\deg(X^{n}Y-1)\geq 0. Since X−1=U⁡(Xn​Y−1)X-1=U(X^{n}Y-1), we also see that deg⁡(X−1)≥0\deg(X-1)\geq 0.

There are 2 cases to consider.

Case 1: deg⁡X≥0\deg X\geq 0. Then

which is a contradiction, since x∉ℱ0x\not\in\mathcal{F}_{0}. So the case deg⁡X≥0\deg X\geq 0 cannot occur.

Let T=Xn​Y−1T=X^{n}Y-1, K=k⁡(X)=k⁡(y)K=k(X)=k(y) and BK=K⊗kBB_{K}=K\otimes_{k}B. Since the generic fiber of X=c​yX=cy is 𝔸∗1​(K)\mathbb{A}^{1}_{*}(K), we see that BK≅K[±1]B_{K}\cong K^{[\pm 1]}. Specifically:

BK=K⁡[x,y,u]=K⁡[x,u]=K⁡[y−1​(t+1),(y−1−1)​t−1+y−1]=K⁡[t,t−1]B_{K}=K[x,y,u]=K[x,u]=K[y^{-1}(t+1),(y^{-1}-1)t^{-1}+y^{-1}]=K[t,t^{-1}]

and

4.4. Degree-Rigidity of BnB_{n}

Theorem 4.2.

BnB_{n} is degree-rigid for each n≥1n\geq 1.

Proof.

Let Bn=k⁡[x,y,(x−1)/(xn​y−1)]B_{n}=k[x,y,(x-1)/(x^{n}y-1)], let δ:Bn→ℕ∪{−∞}\delta:B_{n}\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{-\infty\} be a non-negative degree function, and let Bn=⋃i∈ℕℱiB_{n}=\bigcup_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_{i} be the filtration induced by δ\delta. Given λ,μ∈k\lambda,\mu\in k and f∈Bn∖kf\in B_{n}\setminus k, since k∗⊂ℱ0k^{*}\subset\mathcal{F}_{0}, we have:

0≤δ⁡(f−λ)=δ⁡((f−μ)+(μ−λ))≤max⁡{δ⁡(f−μ),δ⁡(λ−μ)}=δ⁡(f−μ)0\leq\delta(f-\lambda)=\delta((f-\mu)+(\mu-\lambda))\leq\max\{\delta(f-\mu),\delta(\lambda-\mu)\}=\delta(f-\mu)

Therefore, δ⁡(f−λ)=δ⁡(f−μ)\delta(f-\lambda)=\delta(f-\mu) for all f∈B∖kf\in B\setminus k and λ,μ∈k\lambda,\mu\in k. It follows that

0≤δ⁡(x−1xn​y−1)=δ⁡(x−1)−δ⁡(xn​y−1)=δ⁡(x)−δ⁡(xn​y)=δ⁡(x)−n​δ​(x)−δ⁡(y)0\leq\delta\left(\frac{x-1}{x^{n}y-1}\right)=\delta(x-1)-\delta(x^{n}y-1)=\delta(x)-\delta(x^{n}y)=\delta(x)-n\delta(x)-\delta(y)

which gives:

0≤(n−1)​δ​(x)≤−δ⁡(y)⟹(n−1)​δ​(x)=δ⁡(y)=00\leq(n-1)\delta(x)\leq-\delta(y)\implies(n-1)\delta(x)=\delta(y)=0

If n≥2n\geq 2, we see that δ⁡(x)=0\delta(x)=0. If n=1n=1, there is an automorphism α\alpha of B1B_{1} such that α⁡(y)=x\alpha(y)=x. Therefore, δ⁡(x)=0\delta(x)=0 if n=1n=1.

So in all cases, δ⁡(x)=δ⁡(y)=0\delta(x)=\delta(y)=0, meaning that k⁡[x,y]⊂ℱ0k[x,y]\subset\mathcal{F}_{0}. By Proposition 2(c), ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} is factorially closed, and thus algebraically closed, in BnB_{n}. Therefore, the algebraic closure of k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] in BnB_{n} is contained in ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0}, which implies Bn⊂ℱ0B_{n}\subset\mathcal{F}_{0}, i.e., Bn=ℱ0B_{n}=\mathcal{F}_{0}. ∎

Corollary 4.3.

Given integers m,n,d≥1m,n,d\geq 1, if Bm[d]≅kBn[d]B_{m}^{[d]}\cong_{k}B_{n}^{[d]}, then m=nm=n.

Proof.

By Theorem 4.2, BmB_{m} is degree-rigid. Therefore, by Lemma 2.3, BmB_{m} is strongly invariant. Since Bm[d]≅kBn[d]B_{m}^{[d]}\cong_{k}B_{n}^{[d]}, we have Bm≅kBnB_{m}\cong_{k}B_{n}. By Theorem 4.1, it follows that m=nm=n. ∎

=\displaystyle= y⁡(u​v−1)+(u+1)\displaystyle y(uv-1)+(u+1)

and v​y−(x−1)=0vy-(x-1)=0, which implies I⊂JI\subset J. Hence I=JI=J.

Define the kk-isomorphism φ:B→k⁡[X,Y,U,V]≅k[4]\varphi:B\to k[X,Y,U,V]\cong k^{[4]} by φ⁡(x,y,u,v)=(U,V,−Y,−X)\varphi(x,y,u,v)=(U,V,-Y,-X). Then:

Theorem 5.1.

For the surfaces VnV_{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, the following properties hold.

  • (a)

    Vn∈𝒮0V_{n}\in\mathscr{S}_{0} for each n≥1n\geq 1

  • (b)

Question. Over the field k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, are the surfaces VnV_{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, pairwise analytically isomorphic (respectively, pairwise homeomorphic)?
